learn: The k-armed bandit problem and the action value q*(a)
Sample-average estimates and greedy action selection
ε-greedy exploration, with worked probability and sequence examples
The incremental update and its constant-step-size version for nonstationary problems
Three smarter exploration strategies: optimistic initial values, UCB and gradient bandits
intro.why: Bandits isolate the exploration–exploitation dilemma in its simplest form: one state, many actions. Every technique here (incremental estimates, ε-greedy, UCB, softmax policies with baselines) reappears in full RL and in deep RL.
prereq: Session M1 (rewards, values, the update new = old + α(target − old))
Expected value and the normal distribution

sections.title: The k-armed bandit problem
sections.plain: Choose repeatedly among k slot machines to win as much as possible.
sections.body:
You repeatedly choose one of $k$ actions. After each choice you receive a numerical reward drawn from a stationary distribution that depends on the action. The goal is to maximise total reward over, say, 1,000 steps. Each action has a true value, its expected reward:

$$q_*(a) \doteq \mathbb E\,[R_t \mid A_t = a]$$

If we knew $q_*$, we would always pick $\arg\max_a q_*(a)$. We don't, so we keep estimates $Q_t(a)$. Choosing the action with the highest estimate is exploiting; choosing another is exploring. Exploiting maximises the next reward; exploring may produce greater total reward later. This is a nonassociative problem: there is only one situation, so the best action does not depend on a state.

sections.title: Sample averages and greedy selection
sections.plain: Estimate each arm by the average reward it has paid; pick the highest.
sections.body:
$$Q_t(a) \doteq \frac{\text{sum of rewards when } a \text{ taken before } t}{\text{number of times } a \text{ taken before } t} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{t-1} R_i\,\mathbb 1_{A_i=a}}{\sum_{i=1}^{t-1} \mathbb 1_{A_i=a}}$$

$\mathbb 1_{\text{predicate}}$ is 1 if the predicate is true and 0 otherwise; if the denominator is 0, use a default such as 0. By the law of large numbers $Q_t(a) \to q_*(a)$ as the count grows.

Greedy selection: $A_t \doteq \arg\max_a Q_t(a)$, ties broken randomly. Greedy never samples apparently inferior actions, so it can lock onto a mediocre arm forever if early rewards happened to be unlucky for the best one.

sections.title: ε-greedy exploration
sections.plain: Act greedily most of the time; with small probability ε pick at random.
sections.body:
With probability $1-\varepsilon$ take the greedy action; with probability $\varepsilon$ pick uniformly among all actions (including the greedy one). In the limit every action is sampled infinitely often, so every $Q_t(a)$ converges.

Worked example 1. Two actions, $\varepsilon = 0.5$. Probability of the greedy action:

$$P(\text{greedy}) = (1-\varepsilon)\cdot 1 + \varepsilon\cdot\tfrac{1}{k} = 0.5 + 0.5\times 0.5 = 0.75$$

Worked example 2. Four arms, sample averages, all $Q_1 = 0$. Sequence $A_1{=}1,R_1{=}1;\ A_2{=}2,R_2{=}1;\ A_3{=}2,R_3{=}2;\ A_4{=}2,R_4{=}2;\ A_5{=}3,R_5{=}0$.

  • t = 1: all tied, any action is greedy → possibly random.
  • t = 2: $Q=(1,0,0,0)$, greedy is arm 1 but arm 2 chosen → definitely exploring.
  • t = 3: $Q(1)=Q(2)=1$, tie → possibly greedy.
  • t = 4: $Q(2)=1.5$ is the max → possibly greedy.
  • t = 5: $Q(2)\approx1.67$ is the max but arm 3 chosen → definitely exploring.

Answer: definitely exploring at t = 2 and 5; possibly at t = 1, 3, 4 (a random pick can coincide with the greedy one).

sections.title: The 10-armed testbed
sections.plain: Compare methods averaged over 2,000 random bandit problems.
sections.body:
To compare methods fairly: generate 2,000 random 10-armed problems; in each, $q_*(a) \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$, and selecting $a$ yields $R_t \sim \mathcal N(q_*(a), 1)$. Run each method for 1,000 steps on every problem and average the learning curves.

Code example ex1 (last 100 of 1,000 steps):

MethodAverage reward% optimal action
Greedy1.0235%
ε = 0.011.3262%
ε = 0.11.4081%

Greedy improves fastest at the very start, then stalls. ε = 0.1 explores more and finds the optimal arm sooner, but can never exceed about 91% optimal because it keeps exploring; ε = 0.01 improves more slowly but would eventually overtake it. The advantage of exploration grows with reward noise; with deterministic rewards greedy could identify each arm's value after one try (though nonstationarity would still call for exploration).

sections.title: Incremental implementation
sections.plain: Update the average with each new reward instead of storing them all.
sections.body:
Storing all rewards to recompute averages grows memory and computation without bound. For one action, with $Q_n$ the average of its first $n-1$ rewards:

$$Q_{n+1} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}R_i = Q_n + \frac1n\big[R_n - Q_n\big]$$

This is the general form $\text{New} \leftarrow \text{Old} + \text{StepSize}\,[\text{Target} - \text{Old}]$ with step size $1/n$. Only $Q_n$ and $n$ need storing.

Worked example. Rewards 10, 0, 8: $Q_2 = 10$; $Q_3 = 10 + \tfrac12(0-10) = 5$; $Q_4 = 5 + \tfrac13(8-5) = 6$ (the average of 10, 0, 8).

Simple bandit algorithm
  1. For a = 1..k: Q(a) ← 0, N(a) ← 0.
  2. Loop: A ← argmax Q(a) with probability 1 − ε (ties random), else a random action.
  3. R ← bandit(A); N(A) ← N(A) + 1; Q(A) ← Q(A) + [R − Q(A)] / N(A).

sections.title: Nonstationary problems and constant step size
sections.plain: When arm values drift, weight recent rewards more by keeping α fixed.
sections.body:
If true values change over time, it makes sense to give more weight to recent rewards. Use a constant $\alpha \in (0,1]$:

$$Q_{n+1} = Q_n + \alpha[R_n - Q_n] = (1-\alpha)^n Q_1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha(1-\alpha)^{n-i} R_i$$

The weights $(1-\alpha)^n + \sum_i \alpha(1-\alpha)^{n-i} = 1$, and they decay exponentially into the past: an exponential recency-weighted average.

Worked example ($\alpha=0.5$, $Q_1=0$, rewards 10, 0, 8, 4): $Q$ = 5 → 2.5 → 5.25 → 4.625. Weights on rewards 10, 0, 8, 4: 0.0625, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5; weight on $Q_1$: 0.0625. Check: $0.0625\cdot10 + 0.25\cdot8 + 0.5\cdot4 = 4.625$.

Convergence conditions. Estimates converge with probability 1 if $\sum_n\alpha_n = \infty$ (steps big enough to overcome initial conditions) and $\sum_n\alpha_n^2 < \infty$ (steps eventually small enough to settle). $1/n$ satisfies both; a constant α violates the second, which is exactly what lets it keep tracking a moving target. Unlike the sample average, constant-α estimates are biased by $Q_1$; the bias fades as $(1-\alpha)^n$ but never vanishes completely.

sections.title: Optimistic initial values
sections.plain: Start every estimate too high so the agent is disappointed into trying everything.
sections.body:
All methods so far depend on $Q_1(a)$. Setting $Q_1(a) = +5$ on the testbed (where $q_*(a) \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$) is wildly optimistic. Whichever action is tried first pays far less than 5, the estimate drops, and the greedy agent switches to another, still-optimistic action. Every action is tried several times before estimates settle: exploration without randomness.

Code example ex1 (constant $\alpha = 0.1$): optimistic greedy reaches 84.5% optimal actions over the last 100 steps vs 76.7% for realistic ε-greedy with ε = 0.1, despite worse performance at the very start.

Limitation. The drive to explore is temporary: it happens only at the beginning. If the task changes later (nonstationary), nothing renews exploration. Treat it as a simple trick for stationary problems, not a general exploration method.

sections.title: Upper-confidence-bound action selection
sections.plain: Prefer arms that are either good or under-explored.
sections.body:
ε-greedy explores indiscriminately. UCB explores according to the potential of each action to be optimal, taking uncertainty into account:

$$A_t \doteq \arg\max_a \left[\,Q_t(a) + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N_t(a)}}\,\right]$$

If $N_t(a) = 0$, $a$ is treated as maximising (tried first). The square-root term measures uncertainty: it shrinks each time $a$ is selected (denominator grows) and grows slowly for actions not selected ($\ln t$ in the numerator). $c > 0$ controls the degree of exploration. In ex2, UCB with $c = 1$ reached 91% optimal actions on the testbed, versus 81% for ε-greedy with ε = 0.1.

UCB is harder to extend beyond bandits: nonstationary problems and large state spaces (needing function approximation) complicate the counts.

sections.title: Gradient bandits and associative search
sections.plain: Learn preferences, not values, and convert them to probabilities with a softmax.
sections.body:
Learn a numerical preference $H_t(a)$ per action; only relative preferences matter. Actions are chosen by a softmax:

$$\pi_t(a) \doteq \Pr\{A_t=a\} = \frac{e^{H_t(a)}}{\sum_{b=1}^k e^{H_t(b)}}$$

After taking $A_t$ and receiving $R_t$, update by stochastic gradient ascent on expected reward:

$$H_{t+1}(A_t) = H_t(A_t) + \alpha(R_t - \bar R_t)(1-\pi_t(A_t)),\qquad H_{t+1}(a) = H_t(a) - \alpha(R_t-\bar R_t)\pi_t(a)\ \ (a\ne A_t)$$

$\bar R_t$, the average of rewards so far, is a baseline: a reward above it raises the chosen action's probability, below it lowers it. Worked: three actions with $H=0$ (so $\pi=\tfrac13$ each), $A_t = 2$, $R_t = 2$, $\bar R_t = 1$, $\alpha = 0.1$: $H(2) = 0 + 0.1\cdot1\cdot\tfrac23 = 0.0667$, others $-0.0333$; new $\pi \approx (0.322, 0.356, 0.322)$. In ex2, with true means near +4, the baseline version reaches 84% optimal; without it only 51%.

Value-based vs policy-based. Greedy, ε-greedy, optimistic and UCB act on value estimates; the gradient bandit learns a policy directly, the seed of policy-gradient methods (M11).

Associative search (contextual bandits). If the situation changes and the agent can see a clue (e.g. the colour of the machine), it should learn a policy mapping situations to best actions. If actions also affect the next situation, the problem becomes the full RL problem: the MDP of the next session.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Bandits in production. A/B testing, ad selection, recommendation and clinical trial allocation are bandit problems; contextual bandits (e.g. LinUCB) use user features as the "situation".
  • Thompson sampling (posterior sampling) is a popular Bayesian alternative to UCB: sample a plausible value per arm from its posterior and act greedily on the samples.
  • Regret (reward lost compared with always pulling the best arm) is the standard theoretical yardstick; UCB-type algorithms achieve regret growing only logarithmically in t.
  • ε annealing: decaying ε over time combines early exploration with later exploitation; DQN does exactly this.

code.title: 10-armed testbed: greedy, ε-greedy and optimistic initial values
code.explain: Vectorised over 2,000 problems: incremental sample-average (or constant-α) updates, ε-greedy with random tie-breaking; then the three worked examples (0.75, sample averages 10→5→6, constant α 5→2.5→5.25→4.625 with weights).
mistakes: Breaking ties by always taking the first arm.
Measuring only average reward, not % optimal action.
code.notes: Averaging over many problems removes the luck of one run, which is why bandit papers plot averaged curves.
code.code:
"""The 10-armed testbed: greedy vs epsilon-greedy with sample-average estimates.

2,000 random bandit problems; true values q*(a) ~ N(0, 1); a pull of arm a pays N(q*(a), 1).
Each method runs 1,000 steps per problem; we average reward and % optimal action.
Also reproduces three small worked examples from the session.
"""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
P, T, K = 2000, 1000, 10

def run(eps, q0=0.0, alpha=None):
    q = rng.normal(0, 1, (P, K)); best = q.argmax(1)
    Q = np.full((P, K), float(q0)); N = np.zeros((P, K))
    avg_r, opt = np.zeros(T), np.zeros(T)
    rows = np.arange(P)
    for t in range(T):
        greedy = (Q + rng.random((P, K)) * 1e-9).argmax(1)          # random tie-break
        a = np.where(rng.random(P) < eps, rng.integers(0, K, P), greedy)
        r = rng.normal(q[rows, a], 1)
        N[rows, a] += 1
        step = 1 / N[rows, a] if alpha is None else alpha
        Q[rows, a] += step * (r - Q[rows, a])                        # incremental update
        avg_r[t], opt[t] = r.mean(), (a == best).mean()
    return avg_r, opt

print(f"{'method':<28}{'avg reward (last 100)':>22}{'% optimal (last 100)':>22}")
for name, kw in [("greedy (eps = 0)", dict(eps=0)), ("eps = 0.01", dict(eps=0.01)), ("eps = 0.1", dict(eps=0.1)),
                 ("optimistic Q1=5, greedy, a=.1", dict(eps=0, q0=5, alpha=0.1)), ("realistic Q1=0, eps=.1, a=.1", dict(eps=0.1, alpha=0.1))]:
    r, o = run(**kw)
    print(f"{name:<28}{r[-100:].mean():22.3f}{100 * o[-100:].mean():21.1f}%")

print("\nWorked: P(greedy action) with eps=0.5, k=2 =", 1 * (1 - 0.5) + 0.5 * (1 / 2))
Q, n = 0.0, 0
for R in [10, 0, 8]:
    n += 1; Q += (R - Q) / n; print(f"  sample average after reward {R}: Q = {Q:g}")
Q, a = 0.0, 0.5
for R in [10, 0, 8, 4]:
    Q += a * (R - Q); print(f"  constant alpha=0.5 after reward {R}: Q = {Q:g}")
print("  weights on rewards 10,0,8,4 (alpha .5, n=4):", [a * (1 - a) ** (4 - i) for i in range(1, 5)], "weight on Q1:", (1 - a) ** 4)

code.title: UCB and the gradient bandit
code.explain: UCB with several c values; the gradient bandit with and without a baseline on a testbed whose rewards are shifted to around +4; and one hand-checkable preference update.
mistakes: Forgetting the (1 − π) factor for the chosen arm.
code.notes: The baseline does not change the expected gradient, only its variance; the same idea appears in REINFORCE with baseline (M11).
code.code:
"""UCB and the gradient bandit on the 10-armed testbed.

UCB picks argmax Q(a) + c*sqrt(ln t / N(a)); untried arms are picked first.
The gradient bandit keeps preferences H(a), acts by softmax, and updates
H(At) += alpha (R - Rbar)(1 - pi(At)), H(a) -= alpha (R - Rbar) pi(a) for a != At.
"""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
P, T, K = 1000, 1000, 10

def ucb(c):
    q = rng.normal(0, 1, (P, K)); best = q.argmax(1); rows = np.arange(P)
    Q, N, opt, rew = np.zeros((P, K)), np.zeros((P, K)), 0, 0
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        bonus = np.where(N == 0, np.inf, c * np.sqrt(np.log(t) / np.maximum(N, 1)))
        a = (Q + bonus + rng.random((P, K)) * 1e-9).argmax(1)
        r = rng.normal(q[rows, a], 1); N[rows, a] += 1; Q[rows, a] += (r - Q[rows, a]) / N[rows, a]
        if t > T - 100: opt += (a == best).mean(); rew += r.mean()
    return rew / 100, opt

def gradient(alpha, baseline=True):
    q = rng.normal(4, 1, (P, K)); best = q.argmax(1); rows = np.arange(P)   # mean +4: baseline matters
    H, Rbar, opt = np.zeros((P, K)), np.zeros(P), 0
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        pi = np.exp(H - H.max(1, keepdims=True)); pi /= pi.sum(1, keepdims=True)
        a = (pi.cumsum(1) > rng.random((P, 1))).argmax(1)
        r = rng.normal(q[rows, a], 1)
        if baseline: Rbar += (r - Rbar) / t
        one = np.zeros((P, K)); one[rows, a] = 1
        H += alpha * (r - (Rbar if baseline else 0))[:, None] * (one - pi)
        if t > T - 100: opt += (a == best).mean()
    return opt

for c in (0.5, 1, 2, 4):
    r, o = ucb(c); print(f"UCB c={c:<3}: avg reward {r:.3f}, optimal action {o:.1f}%")
for al in (0.1, 0.4):
    print(f"gradient bandit alpha={al}: with baseline {gradient(al):.1f}% optimal, without {gradient(al, False):.1f}%")

# one gradient-bandit update by hand
H = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]); pi = np.exp(H) / np.exp(H).sum(); At, R, Rbar, al = 1, 2.0, 1.0, 0.1
Hn = H - al * (R - Rbar) * pi; Hn[At] = H[At] + al * (R - Rbar) * (1 - pi[At])
print("\nworked update: pi =", pi.round(3), "-> H =", Hn.round(4), "-> new pi =", (np.exp(Hn) / np.exp(Hn).sum()).round(4))
